jobsSalesForecastWeight.citation: Staffing combines realized firm sales with the regional demand forecast; Hamermesh and Pfann (1996), Adjustment Costs in Factor Demand, Journal of Economic Literature. Calibration checked jointly against BLS JOLTS hires, quits, and layoffs, not used as actor rates.

spread.unit: share of staffing forecast from smoothed realized sales
spread.citation: Sensitivity range for a forecast combining paid sales and macro/regional demand.

jobsStaffGapActedPerMonth.citation: Firms close roughly a third of an employment gap per quarter (Hamermesh 1989, AER; Hamermesh and Pfann 1996, JEL); checked against JOLTS hires and layoffs.

spread.unit: share of the staffing gap per month
spread.citation: Firms close roughly a third of an employment gap per quarter (Hamermesh 1989, AER; Hamermesh and Pfann 1996, JEL); checked against JOLTS hires and layoffs.

jobsCashCoverMonths.citation: A business hires with its own cash in reach of a few months of payroll (Federal Reserve Small Business Credit Survey cash-buffer findings).

spread.citation: A business hires with its own cash in reach of a few months of payroll (Federal Reserve Small Business Credit Survey cash-buffer findings).

jobsPayGapWeight.citation: A worker paid well below the going rate for their job looks around; checked against JOLTS quits.

spread.citation: A worker paid well below the going rate for their job looks around; checked against JOLTS quits.

jobsMoneyBufferWeight.citation: Savings let a worker leave work; checked against JOLTS quits.

spread.citation: Savings let a worker leave work; checked against JOLTS quits.

jobsLookBaseline.citation: How far looking sits below staying before pay; checked against JOLTS quits.

spread.citation: How far looking sits below staying before pay; checked against JOLTS quits.

jobsApplyPayWeight.citation: How strongly pay against what a seeker has (or had) draws an application.

spread.citation: How strongly pay against what a seeker has (or had) draws an application.

jobsUnemployedNeedWeight.citation: A seeker without work wants work.

spread.citation: A seeker without work wants work.

jobsSearchFatigueWeeks.citation: Weeks of looking after which a jobless seeker's push to apply is half its starting size. Krueger and Mueller 2011 (Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, a weekly survey of 6,025 unemployed workers) report that the time devoted to job search declines sharply over the spell of unemployment (from the abstract; their earlier time-use paper finds it flat for workers ineligible for benefits, so the size is not sourced). Set near the CPS median spell of about nine weeks.

spread.citation: From a month, when search effort is still near its start, to the CPS long-term cutoff of 26 weeks.

jobsAcceptBaseline.citation: An offer in hand sits slightly above declining before pay.

spread.citation: An offer in hand sits slightly above declining before pay.

jobsFitExperienceWeight.citation: Employers weigh experience in the same occupation (Lazear and Oyer 2013, Handbook of Organizational Economics).

spread.unit: score per year in the occupation
spread.citation: Employers weigh experience in the same occupation (Lazear and Oyer 2013, Handbook of Organizational Economics).

jobsKeepTenureWeight.citation: Tenure and firm-specific skill make an employer keep a worker (Topel 1991, JPE).

spread.citation: Tenure and firm-specific skill make an employer keep a worker (Topel 1991, JPE).

jobsRateWeight.citation: Module reasons outweigh one trait pull in the shared chooser.

spread.citation: Module reasons outweigh one trait pull in the shared chooser.
The fit's neighbors: -0.1 gives take-up 0.61 to 0.75 and 0.14 gives 0.58 to 0.85 in the three towns below.

benefitsFileBase.citation: How readily an eligible worker files for unemployment insurance before the benefit's share of the lost pay, the layoff's stress and their traits are weighed (jobs-benefits.ts filingDecision). Take-up among eligible unemployed workers: 0.734 mean, SD 0.201, over 714 state-years 2002-15 (Auray & Fuller, Quantitative Economics 2020, Table 1); 77% over 1989-2012 (Auray, Fuller & Lkhagvasuren 2018); a literature range of 0.55 to 0.83 (Anderson & Meyer, NBER WP 4787). Fitted with benefitsFileReplacementWeight over every business worker (full and counted) of three drawn towns with at least 100, each laid off in thought from their own job: Wayland, Michigan (2684880, seed 0c4eea785dc2), Piltzville, Montana (3057475, seed b3ab1b16e0f7) and Washington, District of Columbia (1150000, seed ed36e0484fc6), label trait-wiring, built January 20, 2025: take-up 0.73 in Wayland and 0.76 in Washington. Piltzville reads 0.46 because Montana's law row gives a benefit of 0.26 of the lost pay (pool item laws-unemployment-share-basis-mt-co).

spread.unit: score per log of the benefit's share of the lost pay
spread.citation: The fit's neighbors with the base refitted: 0.4 gives elasticities of 0.30 to 0.46 and 0.6 about 0.45 to 0.60 in the three towns of benefitsFileBase.

benefitsFileReplacementWeight.citation: How much the share of the lost weekly pay the benefit replaces pulls an eligible worker toward filing, as the log of the share (jobs-benefits.ts filingDecision). A 10% higher weekly benefit raises take-up 4.7%: elasticity 0.467, 95% CI 0.382 to 0.553 (McQuillan & Moore, Washington ESD working paper, Nov 2025, https://esd.wa.gov/media/pdf/4240/endogenoustake-upuibenefts-working-paper-nov2025pdf); Anderson & Meyer (NBER WP 4787) report 0.46 to 0.78. At 0.5, raising every benefit by 10% raises take-up by an elasticity of 0.45 (Wayland), 0.42 (Piltzville) and 0.52 (Washington) over every business worker (full and counted) of three drawn towns with at least 100, each laid off in thought from their own job: Wayland, Michigan (2684880, seed 0c4eea785dc2), Piltzville, Montana (3057475, seed b3ab1b16e0f7) and Washington, District of Columbia (1150000, seed ed36e0484fc6), label trait-wiring, built January 20, 2025. The share is the state's weekly share of pay up to its weekly maximum, so a high earner capped at the maximum files less.

jobsEnterBaseline.citation: How far starting to look sits below staying out before money pressure, for a full person and a counted adult alike; checked against CPS flows into the labor force and the region's unemployment rate (in two drawn towns, counted seekers settle at about 5% to 7% of the counted jobs; at -1.5 they were about twice the jobs).

spread.citation: CPS labor force flows, 1990-2019.

jobsEarliestRetirementAge.citation: 42 U.S.C. 402(a), 416(l): Social Security retirement benefits start at 62 at the earliest.

jobsRetireBaseline.citation: How far retiring sits below staying at 62 before age and savings, so that the chooser's comparison against staying puts most workers out of work by their mid-60s with the poorest and the youngest last; checked against CPS labor force participation by age (about 57% at 62-64, 26% at 65-69, BLS 2019). At -3 and 0.6 the first generated-world month (Landrum, July 2022) retired 63 of about 2,300 workers at once, far above CPS exits at 65-69.

spread.citation: BLS CPS participation by age, 2015-2019.

jobsRetireAgeWeight.citation: Each year past 62 pulls further toward retiring; checked against CPS participation falling from 62 to 70.

spread.citation: BLS CPS participation by age, 2015-2019.

jobsOlderWorkWebWeight.citation: How strongly the outcome web's factor on older workers' employment (labor.older-employment) pulls people from the earliest to the full retirement age to stay at work or start looking: the weight times the log of the factor, on the retire, leave and enter choices. Checked against the retirement-age link's researched size, a 10 percent rise in the employment share at 62 to 66 for a two-year rise in the full retirement age (range 4 to 22 percent; Mastrobuoni 2009, Journal of Public Economics), in one played year of twin bench worlds.

spread.citation: The weights that put the year's move near the ends of the link's range, 4 and 22 percent, in the fitting runs: Sparks, Nevada (1.8 percent at 1, 13.6 at 6), Dakota Dunes, South Dakota (5.3 at 4, 8.6 at 5) and Hudson, New Hampshire.

jobsOnTheJobSearchMonths.citation: How long an employed person keeps looking before giving up for now; on-the-job search spells are short (Faberman, Mueller, Sahin and Topa 2022, Survey of Consumer Expectations job search supplement).

spread.citation: How long an employed person keeps looking before giving up for now; on-the-job search spells are short (Faberman, Mueller, Sahin and Topa 2022, Survey of Consumer Expectations job search supplement).

jobsBenefitWeeklyShare.citation: U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration, Significant Provisions of State Unemployment Insurance Laws, January 2026 and July 2026 (53 programs, as gathered in OPUS-GOV's starting law).
jobsBenefitWeeklyShare.estimatedFrom: Fill-in for a program whose law row records no benefit fraction (Alaska's weighted schedule): most states pay 1/26 of high-quarter wages, about half the weekly wage.

spread.citation: U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration, Significant Provisions of State Unemployment Insurance Laws, January 2026 and July 2026 (53 programs, as gathered in OPUS-GOV's starting law).

jobsBenefitMinimumBasePeriodMinor.citation: U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration, Significant Provisions of State Unemployment Insurance Laws, January 2026 and July 2026 (53 programs, as gathered in OPUS-GOV's starting law).
jobsBenefitMinimumBasePeriodMinor.estimatedFrom: Fill-in for a program whose law row records no base-period or high-quarter minimum: median minimum base-period wages across the state programs, July 2026.

spread.citation: U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration, Significant Provisions of State Unemployment Insurance Laws, January 2026 and July 2026 (53 programs, as gathered in OPUS-GOV's starting law).

jobsQuitToNonemploymentShare.citation: About half of quits go straight to another job and half to unemployment or out of the labor force (Fallick and Fleischman 2004, CPS job-to-job flows; BLS CPS gross flows E to U and E to N).

spread.citation: About half of quits go straight to another job and half to unemployment or out of the labor force (Fallick and Fleischman 2004, CPS job-to-job flows; BLS CPS gross flows E to U and E to N).

jobsQuitBaseline.citation: The pull to quit to nothing for a worker at the typical tenure, paid the going rate, in a place at the natural unemployment rate. Calibrated so the summed pulls reproduce half the JOLTS total-private quit rate (1.906% a month, 2001-2019, half going to unemployment or out of the labor force: Fallick and Fleischman 2004); the test checks the total, no rate picks a worker.

spread.unit: logit of a month's pull to quit
spread.citation: The pull to quit to nothing for a worker at the typical tenure, paid the going rate, in a place at the natural unemployment rate. Calibrated so the summed pulls reproduce half the JOLTS total-private quit rate (1.906% a month, 2001-2019, half going to unemployment or out of the labor force: Fallick and Fleischman 2004); the test checks the total, no rate picks a worker.

jobsTypicalTenureYears.citation: BLS Employee Tenure in 2024, median tenure of wage and salary workers (about 3.9 years).

jobsQuitTenureWeight.citation: Short-tenure workers quit far more often than long-tenure ones (BLS Employee Tenure; Farber 1994, JOLE): each log step of tenure below the typical raises the pull; checked against JOLTS quits by industry.

spread.unit: logit per log-year of tenure below the typical
spread.citation: Short-tenure workers quit far more often than long-tenure ones (BLS Employee Tenure; Farber 1994, JOLE): each log step of tenure below the typical raises the pull; checked against JOLTS quits by industry.

jobsUnemploymentQuitWeight.citation: Quits fall when unemployment rises: JOLTS total private quits fell from about 2.2% (2007) to 1.2% (2009) while unemployment rose about 4.7 points (BLS JOLTS, LNS14000000).

spread.unit: logit per point of unemployment above the natural rate
spread.citation: Quits fall when unemployment rises: JOLTS total private quits fell from about 2.2% (2007) to 1.2% (2009) while unemployment rose about 4.7 points (BLS JOLTS, LNS14000000).

jobsUnemploymentLookWeight.citation: On-the-job search falls when jobs are scarce (Faberman, Mueller, Sahin and Topa 2022); checked against JOLTS quits and hires through the cycle.

spread.unit: score per point of unemployment above the natural rate
spread.citation: On-the-job search falls when jobs are scarce (Faberman, Mueller, Sahin and Topa 2022); checked against JOLTS quits and hires through the cycle.

jobsUnemploymentEntryWeight.citation: Discouraged-worker effect: fewer enter the labor force when the local unemployment rate is high (BLS CPS participation through the 2007-2010 recession).

spread.unit: logit per point of unemployment above the natural rate
spread.citation: Discouraged-worker effect: fewer enter the labor force when the local unemployment rate is high (BLS CPS participation through the 2007-2010 recession).

jobsSwitchCost.citation: Changing employers costs something (lost tenure, search, relocation of routine): job-to-job movers gain on the order of 5 to 10 percent in pay (Topel and Ward 1992, QJE; Fallick and Fleischman 2004). With the accept baseline of 0.5 and an apply pay weight of 8, a worker needs about a 6 percent raise, or a trait pull, to move.

spread.unit: score for an employed worker taking another job
spread.citation: Changing employers costs something (lost tenure, search, relocation of routine): job-to-job movers gain on the order of 5 to 10 percent in pay (Topel and Ward 1992, QJE; Fallick and Fleischman 2004). With the accept baseline of 0.5 and an apply pay weight of 8, a worker needs about a 6 percent raise, or a trait pull, to move.

jobsWithdrawActedPerMonth.citation: An employer that has all the staff it wants lets its open postings lapse over a couple of months rather than at once; vacancies stay open about a month on average (BLS JOLTS vacancy duration, DHI).

spread.unit: open positions withdrawn per position of surplus, per month
spread.citation: An employer that has all the staff it wants lets its open postings lapse over a couple of months rather than at once; vacancies stay open about a month on average (BLS JOLTS vacancy duration, DHI).

jobsOfferDays.citation: How long an employer holds a job offer open before withdrawing it. Common practice is a few days for hourly work up to about two weeks for professional offers; NACE's Principles for Ethical Professional Practice ask employers to give students reasonable time to decide. Checked against played offers lapsing unanswered only when the player has no explicit control.

spread.citation: How long an employer holds a job offer open before withdrawing it. Common practice is a few days for hourly work up to about two weeks for professional offers; NACE's Principles for Ethical Professional Practice ask employers to give students reasonable time to decide. Checked against played offers lapsing unanswered only when the player has no explicit control.

jobsFitReferralWeight.citation: Referrals bring a sizable share of hires (Topa 2011, Labor Markets and Referrals, Handbook of Social Economics); the weight is tuned against that share.

spread.citation: Referrals bring a sizable share of hires (Topa 2011, Labor Markets and Referrals, Handbook of Social Economics); the weight is tuned against that share.

jobsReferralDays.citation: A referral helps while the search is live; the median unemployment spell is about ten weeks (Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Population Survey).

spread.citation: A referral helps while the search is live; the median unemployment spell is about ten weeks (Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Population Survey).

jobsOlderApplicantPenalty.citation: Older applicants draw fewer callbacks than younger ones with the same resume (Neumark, Burn and Button 2019, Journal of Political Economy: a large resume field experiment, callbacks for applicants in their mid-sixties well below those for applicants around thirty). Applied as score points taken off an employer's fit for the oldest applicants where no law bars it; three points is three years' experience in the fit score.

spread.unit: fit score at the oldest applicant age
spread.citation: Older applicants draw fewer callbacks than younger ones with the same resume (Neumark, Burn and Button 2019, Journal of Political Economy: a large resume field experiment, callbacks for applicants in their mid-sixties well below those for applicants around thirty). Applied as score points taken off an employer's fit for the oldest applicants where no law bars it; three points is three years' experience in the fit score.

jobsAgeBiasFromAge.citation: Age Discrimination in Employment Act, 29 U.S.C. 631(a): protects workers 40 and older.

jobsAgeBiasFullAge.citation: The oldest age tested in the field experiment (Neumark, Burn and Button 2019): the penalty slides from the protected age to its full size here.

spread.citation: The oldest age tested in the field experiment (Neumark, Burn and Button 2019): the penalty slides from the protected age to its full size here.

jobsAgeLawEmployees.citation: Age Discrimination in Employment Act, 29 U.S.C. 630(b): covers employers with 20 or more employees; a state or local ban reaches smaller ones.

jobsMotherYoungChildYears.citation: Malik 2018 (Center for American Progress), mothers with children under 5, the group the D.C. universal pre-K result is measured on.

jobsAdultAge.citation: Age of majority; a household's children are its members under 18 (Census household definitions).

jobsFullRetirementAge.citation: 42 U.S.C. 416(l): the full Social Security retirement age is 67 for those born in 1960 or later; the upper end of the 62 to 67 group the older-employment outcome covers.

jobsLowWageLineHourlyMinor.citation: $15 an hour in cents: the line of the labor.low-wage-jobs outcome (Economic Policy Institute: 15 percent of workers paid under $15 an hour in 2022).

jobsWeeklyEarningsAllWorkers.citation: BLS Employment Projections, Table 5.1 Unemployment rates and earnings by educational attainment, 2025 annual estimates (11-month averages excluding October), https://www.bls.gov/emp/tables/unemployment-earnings-education.htm: median usual weekly earnings, all workers, $1,268.

jobsWeeklyEarningsLessThanHighSchool.citation: BLS Employment Projections, Table 5.1 Unemployment rates and earnings by educational attainment, 2025 annual estimates (11-month averages excluding October), https://www.bls.gov/emp/tables/unemployment-earnings-education.htm: less than a high school diploma, $770.

jobsWeeklyEarningsNoCollege.citation: BLS Employment Projections, Table 5.1 Unemployment rates and earnings by educational attainment, 2025 annual estimates (11-month averages excluding October), https://www.bls.gov/emp/tables/unemployment-earnings-education.htm: high school diploma, $966 (less than a high school diploma $770).

jobsWeeklyEarningsSomeCollege.citation: BLS Employment Projections, Table 5.1 Unemployment rates and earnings by educational attainment, 2025 annual estimates (11-month averages excluding October), https://www.bls.gov/emp/tables/unemployment-earnings-education.htm: some college no degree $1,062, associate's degree $1,135.
jobsWeeklyEarningsSomeCollege.estimatedFrom: Midpoint of the two rows the survey's 'some college' answer spans (CES some-college covers both).

spread.citation: BLS Employment Projections, Table 5.1 Unemployment rates and earnings by educational attainment, 2025 annual estimates (11-month averages excluding October), https://www.bls.gov/emp/tables/unemployment-earnings-education.htm: some college no degree $1,062 and associate's degree $1,135.

jobsWeeklyEarningsCollege.citation: BLS Employment Projections, Table 5.1 Unemployment rates and earnings by educational attainment, 2025 annual estimates (11-month averages excluding October), https://www.bls.gov/emp/tables/unemployment-earnings-education.htm: bachelor's degree, $1,578 (master's $1,876, professional $2,294, doctoral $2,307).

jobsSchoolingPayShare.citation: The share of the raw earnings gap between education levels that remains within one occupation and employer: positions are already priced for their occupation, which carries part of the schooling premium (a degree opens higher-paid roles).
jobsSchoolingPayShare.estimatedFrom: Assumed share; no source measuring the within-occupation schooling premium was fetched, so it is an estimate with a wide spread, to be researched.

spread.unit: share of the raw weekly-earnings gap
spread.citation: Assumed range around a middle value; unmeasured.

jobsTenureReturnFull.citation: Altonji and Williams 2005, Do Wages Rise with Job Seniority? A Reassessment (ILR Review 58(3); NBER w6010 abstract): "The evidence from the data used by AS and Topel points to an effect of ten years of tenure on the log wage equal to .11", above Altonji and Shakotko's .066 and well below Topel's estimate, and probably biased upward by the wage measure. Read as the long-tenure ceiling of the profile full x (1 - e^(-years / jobsTenureReturnYears)): .11 / (1 - e^(-10/4)) = 0.12 log points.
jobsTenureReturnFull.estimatedFrom: The reconciled ten-year return to tenure (Altonji and Williams 2005), spread over the profile whose shape Buchinsky, Fougere, Kramarz and Tchernis (IZA DP 1521, 2005; Review of Economic Studies 77(3), 2010) Table 8 gives. Checked against totals, not any one worker: a stayer at the BLS median tenure, 3.9 years (jobsTypicalTenureYears), gets 0.12 x (e^(-3.9/4) - e^(-4.9/4)) = 1.0 point a year over the market's move; job stayers' median wage growth ran 3.5 percent in the 12 months to September 2026 (Atlanta Fed Wage Growth Tracker, FRED FRBATLWGT12MMUMHWGJST) against 3.2 percent for ECI wages and salaries in the 12 months to June 2026 (BLS ECI release), and 4.4 against about 3.6 a year earlier.

spread.unit: log points of pay at long tenure
spread.citation: Low: Altonji and Shakotko 1987's .066 at ten years, as Altonji and Williams 2005 quote it, over 0.918. High: Topel 1991 (JPE 99(1); NBER w3294 abstract: "10 years of current job seniority raises the wage of the typical male worker in the U.S. by over 25 percent"), .2323 at ten years in Buchinsky et al.'s Table 8, over 0.918.

jobsTenureReturnYears.citation: Buchinsky, Fougere, Kramarz and Tchernis, Interfirm Mobility, Wages and the Returns to Seniority and Experience in the U.S. (IZA DP 1521, 2005; Review of Economic Studies 77(3), 2010), Table 8, cumulative return to tenure, Altonji-Williams estimator on the PSID: .0528 at 2 years, .0988 at 5, .1195 at 10, .1164 at 15, .1287 at 20; Topel two-step: .0973, .1843, .2323, .2343, .2469.
jobsTenureReturnYears.estimatedFrom: The span of the profile full x (1 - e^(-years / span)) fitted to both columns' shape: at 4 years it reaches 0.43 of its ten-year value at 2 years (the table: 0.44 and 0.42), 0.78 at 5 (0.83 and 0.79) and 1.06 at 15 (0.97 and 1.01), flat after ten as the table is.

spread.citation: At 3 years the profile reaches 0.50 of its ten-year value at 2 years and 0.84 at 5; at 5 years, 0.38 and 0.73: together they bracket Table 8's 0.42 to 0.44 and 0.79 to 0.83 (Buchinsky et al. 2005).

jobsRaisePerWorkYear.citation: WorldatWork 2024-2025 Salary Budget Survey, Figure 17 (United States): in 2023 high performers (24 percent of employees) got a mean merit increase of 4.8 percent, middle performers (59 percent) 3.5 percent and low performers (5 percent) 1.3 percent; Figure 18: the gap between middle and high performers was 1.2 to 1.5 points every year from 2015 to 2024 (2.0 in 2020). Barrick and Mount 1991 (Personnel Psychology 44(1), Table 2): conscientiousness correlates 0.22 with job performance.
jobsRaisePerWorkYear.estimatedFrom: About 1.0 point of merit increase per standard deviation of rated performance (on a normal spread of the rated, the top 24 percent sit about 1.5 deviations above the middle group, 1.3 points apart, and the bottom 5 percent about 1.7 below it, 2.2 points apart), times the 0.22 of rated performance that conscientiousness carries, over the spread of the employer's read of how a person works, 1.28 years (traitWeightJobsValueWorker 4.4 times the 0.29 lean spread within a firm its citation measures): 0.010 x 0.22 / 1.28 = 0.0017 of pay a year per year of that read. A worker one deviation more diligent gets about 0.2 point more a year, about 2 percent more pay after ten years in the job; Gensowski 2018, Personality, IQ, and lifetime earnings (doi:10.1016/j.labeco.2017.12.004), finds 16.7 percent of lifetime earnings per deviation of conscientiousness in the high-IQ Terman sample, which also carries schooling and the jobs people reach, an upper bound this raise stays well under.

spread.unit: share of pay a year per year of how they work
spread.citation: Merit points per deviation of rated performance 0.8 to 1.2 (WorldatWork Figure 18's 1.2 to 2.0 point gaps between performance groups), the trait correlation 0.20 to 0.23 across occupational groups (Barrick and Mount 1991, Table 2) and the lean spread 0.25 to 0.34 across the three places traitWeightJobsValueWorker names.
